content: The Rotavirus Vaccine Program is an initiative aimed at reducing child morbidity and mortality caused by diarrheal diseases through the accelerated availability of rotavirus vaccines specifically designed for use in developing countries. Each year, rotavirus-induced diarrheal disease results in the deaths of over 600,000 children and hospitalizes an additional two million. The majority of these deaths occur in developing nations where access to treatment is limited. However, nearly every child worldwide will experience at least one episode of rotavirus-induced diarrhea by the age of five. The Centers for Disease Control established the Rotavirus Vaccine Program to address this issue by ensuring the availability of a rotavirus vaccine in developing countries. In 1998, a rotavirus vaccine was licensed for use in the United States. Clinical trials conducted in the United States, Finland, and Venezuela demonstrated that the vaccine was 80% to 100% effective in preventing severe diarrhea caused by rotavirus A, with no statistically significant serious adverse effects observed during the trials. However, the vaccine was withdrawn from the market in 1999 after it was discovered that it might increase the risk of intussusception, a form of bowel obstruction, in approximately one out of every 12,000 vaccinated infants. This finding sparked intense debate regarding the relative risks and benefits of the rotavirus vaccine. By 2006, two vaccines against rotavirus A infection were shown to be both safe and effective in children. Rotarix is a live, attenuated human rotavirus vaccine developed by GlaxoSmithKline. It contains a rotavirus strain with G1P specificity and is administered orally. The licensure process for Rotarix is ongoing in the European Union. RotaTeq is a live, oral pentavalent vaccine developed by Merck. It contains five reassortant rotaviruses, which were created by combining genetic material from human and bovine rotavirus parent strains. Four of these reassortant viruses express one of the outer capsid VP7 proteins (serotypes G1, G2, G3, or G4) from the human rotavirus parent strain, while the attachment protein VP4 (type P7) is derived from the bovine rotavirus parent strain. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved RotaTeq for use in the United States. Merck is collaborating with various partners, including the Rotavirus Vaccine Program, PATH (Program for Appropriate Technology in Health), and other governmental and non-governmental organizations, to develop and implement strategies for ensuring access to this vaccine in developing countries.
